title: Map shows the pubs, houses and castles named the most haunted places in Wales
excerpt: Many of Wales' most iconic castles and pubs feature on the list of places where you could get a fright
content:
Many of Wales' most iconic castles and pubs feature on the list of places where you could get a fright

Richard Ault

09:26, 01 Nov 2026

Phantom kitchen saboteurs, spectral soldiers, and Victorian children lingering in shopfronts are among thousands of apparitions reported to be haunting towns and cities.

‌

‌

Author Dr Paul Lee has documented more than 5,500 reported hauntings around the UK over a decade of painstaking research, and they are all included in our interactive map revealing Britain’s most haunted locations.

‌

Halloween may be over, but it appears ghostly goings-on don't just happen on one day each year.

‌

Reports range from everyday oddities – including phantom tobacco smoke and unexplained footsteps – to intense poltergeist claims involving flying plates and airborne kitchen utensils.

According to Dr Lee’s research, Cardiff and Newport are some of Wales' most haunted hotspots, with each city having 12 reported haunted locations each. In the Welsh capital, the New Theatre, Cardiff Castle and the Royal Infirmary are all spooky locations, while in Newport people might expect to have a fright at the Transporter Bridge or one of the city's pubs, including Ye Olde Murenger House and The Carpenters Arms.

At the New Theatre, Dr Lee's research found that a spectral lady is said to haunt one of the boxes here. She is said to have either fallen from it or died in it according to various legends. At the workshop at the Transporter Bridge, tools are said to have gone missing and a bucket was reportedly thrown across a room.

‌

Neath Abbey also makes an appearance on the map, where a phantom monk is said to have been seen making his way from the entrance to the area where the Abbey church was once located. The Eagle Inn in Narberth, Pembrokeshire, is another reportedly haunted pub, where a little boy has been seen in the second floor flat above the pub.

Since Dr Lee started his research, a handful of haunted buildings that he documented no longer exist. However, the spooks described may still linger on.

‌

‌

All the descriptions of paranormal activity on the map have come from Dr Lee’s meticulous research, which, in many cases, includes interviews with witnesses and his own investigations, during which he has visited numerous locations and trawled through various newspaper archives.

Dr Lee said: “Of course, some of the reports in the database could be hoaxes or urban legends; there is no way to know in many cases.”

‌

Dr Lee, who holds a doctorate in nuclear physics, began compiling the national register in 2015 and continues to update the archive.

His recent investigations include the Syderstone Ghost — a series of unexplained night-time disturbances in a Norfolk village that was recently featured in Fortean Times.

Dr Lee has published his findings in several volumes, including the UK Haunted Hospitality series, which investigates more than 2,000 haunted pubs, hotels, and eateries across the country. You can find out more about his research by visiting his website: www.paullee.com/ghosts.
